Procedures:
Parse external strings and data into typed domain objects at system boundaries, before downstream processing.
When translating or re-raising an exception, chain the original exception (for example, with `raise ... from e`) to preserve the debugging trail.
In batch operations, isolate per-item failures so one bad item does not abort the batch; track successes and failures separately, preferably by item or index.
Use specific, appropriate exception types rather than generic Exception; add context where needed.
Validate inputs at API boundaries before expensive processing; report all validation errors at once when practical.
Write error messages that explain what failed, why it failed, and how to fix it, including relevant values or valid options when useful.
Test error paths, including that expected exceptions are raised correctly.
Include useful debugging context, such as identifiers and counts, when logging errors.
Expose batch progress through an optional callback so callers can observe progress without coupling business logic to a UI.
For application-specific failures, create domain-specific exception classes that can carry structured information.
Use Pydantic models for complex structured input validation and automatic structured errors.
Document possible exceptions and failure modes in function docstrings.
